Resolute
REZ-uh-loot
adj. (fixed in purpose; firm; the citizen who has already decided)
From Latin resolutus, the past participle of resolvere, to loose, to untie, and so to settle a question by taking it apart. Webster notes that the Latin adjective does not carry the English sense. English took the word from resolve: a question worked through, then a will fixed. A resolute man is not a man who has never doubted. He is a man who has finished doubting.

Biblical Definition

Resolute is the settled will that remains after the question has been decided. Daniel purposed in his heart before the king’s meat was set before him (Dan 1:8). Joshua did not leave the choice open for his own house: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15). Ruth would not be turned back (Rut 1:16). Paul determined to know nothing among the Corinthians save Christ crucified (1Co 2:2). The three friends at the furnace were “not careful to answer” the king (Dan 3:16) — not careless, but already decided, so the threat had nothing left to negotiate. Peter states the limit of every lesser loyalty: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). Scripture’s word for this estate is steadfastness: “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” (1Co 15:58). Resolve is the decision. Resolute is the man who keeps it when the cost arrives. In this ministry the word names the RESOLUTE Citizen: Responsible, Engaged, Steadfast, Obedient, Loyal, Upright, Trustworthy, Enduring. Those eight words are the duties, not a slogan. A man may be loud about his country and still fail the duties: irresponsible in his own corner, absent from his city, moved by pressure, disobedient to lawful authority, disloyal to his people, crooked where no one is looking, careless with his word, and quit before the work is finished.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines resolute as having a fixed purpose; determined; hence bold, firm, steady, constant in pursuing a purpose. He notes that the Latin resolutus has a different signification, and sends the reader to Resolve.

expand to see more

RES’OLUTE, adjective. [The Latin resolutus has a different signification. See Resolve.] Having a fixed purpose; determined; hence, bold; firm; steady; constant in pursuing a purpose.

Edward is at hand, ready to fight; therefore be resolute.

Key Scripture

Dan 1:8 — "But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself."

Jos 24:15 — "And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."

1Co 15:58 — "Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord."

Act 5:29 — "Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men."

Modern Corruption

Resolute has been cheapened into a mood, a brand, and a political costume — firmness with no prior decision, and no Lord over the decision.

expand to see more

The age uses resolute as a posture. A man is called resolute because he will not yield in an argument, because his jaw is set, or because a campaign needs a word that sounds like courage. Webster’s sense is narrower and better: fixed purpose, constant in pursuing it. Scripture is narrower still. Daniel’s purpose had an object — he would not defile himself. Joshua’s purpose had a Lord. A will fixed on the wrong object is not resoluteness. It is obstinacy.

The other corruption is the opposite: resolve as a January feeling that expires when the cost arrives. Daniel’s purpose was tested at the table, and again at the lions. The three friends were not careful to answer because the answer had already been given. A resolute citizen is not a man who feels strongly about public life. He is a man who has decided, under God, what he will not do and what he will not abandon, and who is still there when the writing is signed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin resolvere, to loose and so to settle; English took the moral sense from resolve. The biblical estate is steadfastness and a purposed heart, not a Latin adjective invented for the feeling.

expand to see more

Latin resolvere (re + solvere) — to loosen, to undo, and so to settle a question by taking it apart.

English resolve — the fixed purpose that remains after the question is settled. Webster sends the reader here, not to the Latin adjective.

Hebrew sum / sim (H7760), in Dan 1:8 — Daniel set it upon his heart. The purpose was placed, not felt.

Greek hedraios (G1476) — seated, steadfast; Paul’s word in 1Co 15:58 for a man who is not moved off his place.

Usage

"A resolute man has finished the question before the threat arrives, as Daniel had purposed before the meat was offered."

"The RESOLUTE Citizen is responsible, engaged, steadfast, obedient, loyal, upright, trustworthy, and enduring — eight duties, not a mood."

"Firmness aimed at the wrong object is not resoluteness. It is a will that refused to be settled by the Lord."
